title: Bimbisara's visit
hookLine: the king offers half his kingdom (Buddhacarita 10)

cards: A city ringed by hills, and a young man in a plain robe walking its streets with a bowl. The poem says people stop what they're doing to look at him. Those walking stand still.
Those standing follow. People at windows lean out. He doesn't look like a beggar, whatever he's carrying.
In a palace above the streets, another king is watching too. He doesn't know who this is. But he wants to.

teach.b: First, the city. The prince has crossed the Ganges and come to Rajagriha, the royal city of Magadha.

He goes for alms, eats what he's given, and climbs a hill outside the town to rest. Second, the king. Bimbisara, king of Magadha, sees him from his palace and sends someone to follow him and find where he stays.
Then he goes himself, up the hill with only a few attendants, and sits down with the young wanderer as an equal. Third, the offer. Bimbisara speaks as a friend.
In paraphrase: I know your family, a great royal line. You're young and strong, and you've left a throne to beg. This doesn't suit you.
Take half of my kingdom. Rule beside me. Then he lays out a sensible plan for a life: youth for pleasure, the middle years for wealth, old age for religion.
Do things in their season. Fourth, the spirit of it. This isn't a trap, and it isn't a bribe.

The poem presents Bimbisara as generous and sincere: he looks at a stranger and sees someone worth half of everything he has, and helps the only way a king knows how. That's what makes this harder than yesterday.
The ministers came to take the prince back. Bimbisara comes to give him more. The prince listens, and doesn't reach for the offer.
His reasons fill the whole next canto. Today, the offer just hangs in the air, held out with an open hand.

how: Bimbisara appears in other Buddhist stories as a king friendly to the Buddha, and the meeting on the hill outside Rajagriha is told in the Pali discourses as well as in this poem.

o: a king's offer of half his realm to the wanderer
a royal envoy sent to bring the prince home
a king's order to arrest the wandering prince

games.q: the visit on the hill: tap the pairs.

s: in the poem, Bimbisara sends soldiers to bring the stranger to the palace
he goes up the hill himself, with a few attendants, and sits with him.
the king's offer is a trick to keep the prince from his search
the poem presents it as generous and sincere.
Bimbisara advises a season for everything: pleasure, then wealth, then religion
youth for enjoying, the middle years for wealth, old age for religion.

games.q: you're a wanderer with a bowl, resting on a hill. a king climbs up, sits beside you as a friend, and offers you half his kingdom. what do you do?
o: accept, and do good with it.
listen, thank him, and don't reach for it.
ask for the whole kingdom instead.
games.why: he hears the king out and doesn't take the offer. his reasons fill the whole next canto of the poem.

practice: Bring to mind an offer you don't want to take, a promotion that would pull you away from what matters, a second helping, a favor with strings, and notice the goodwill in it first.
Let yourself be grateful for the person who offered. Then quietly rehearse a no that keeps the gratitude in it: thank you, truly, and no.

wordCard.voice: Bimbisara's visit. The king of Magadha climbs a hill to meet the wandering prince and, in friendship, offers him half his kingdom. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the name of the king of Magadha; the poem also calls him Shrenya.

carryVoice: Your line: half a kingdom. A king, a wanderer, and an open hand between them. Day seven hundred eleven, done.
